title: Perfect Discrimination of Non-Orthogonal Quantum States via Adaptive Post-Measurement Queries
abstract: A set of pairwise non-orthogonal quantum states cannot be perfectly discriminated, and this remains true even when one bit of classical partial information is available prior to the measurement. Contrary to the usual intuition that earlier information is at least as valuable as later information, we show that the same bit can be more useful when it arrives after the measurement. We present a framework for state discrimination in which the sender provides classical information in response to a request from the receiver, which we refer to as a query. In some cases, pairwise non-orthogonal states can be perfectly discriminated when the query is allowed to depend on the measurement outcome. We give a general method for finding the optimal strategy in this setting, which turns out to be the standard minimum-error discrimination problem for an auxiliary ensemble.
summary: This paper explores the theoretical limit of distinguishing non-orthogonal quantum states when classical information is available. It demonstrates that allowing queries to depend on the measurement outcome (adaptive post-measurement) can yield a higher success probability than having prior knowledge, fundamentally challenging intuition about the value of timing in quantum measurements.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether allowing classical information to arrive adaptively after a quantum measurement can improve the perfect discrimination of non-orthogonal quantum states compared to having that information available beforehand.
main_result: Adaptive post-measurement queries can, in certain cases, allow for the perfect discrimination of pairwise non-orthogonal states, surpassing limits set by pre-measurement knowledge. The optimal strategy relates this problem to standard minimum-error discrimination on an auxiliary ensemble.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework comparing success probabilities ($P_{	ext{pre}}$ vs $P_{	ext{adapt\_post}}$) and derive the optimal measurement strategy by mapping the adaptive query scenario onto a known minimum-error discrimination problem for an auxiliary ensemble ($\mathcal{E}_{	ext{aux}}$).
model_or_system: The model is quantum state discrimination involving a set of pairwise non-orthogonal pure quantum states ($\psi_x$) in a given Hilbert space dimension ($d$). Examples include trine and tetrahedron ensembles.
key_observables: Success probabilities for discrimination: $P_{	ext{pre}}$ (pre-measurement), $P_{	ext{post}}$ (outcome-independent post-measurement), and $P_{	ext{adapt\_post}}$ (adaptive post-measurement query).
important_parameters: The number of states ($n$), the dimension of the Hilbert space ($d$), and the overlap between states ($\langle \psi_i | \psi_j angle$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often focuses on the case where only one bit of classical information is available, and it challenges the intuition that earlier classical information is always superior.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the timing difference between query types (red vs. blue). Figure 2 provides a graphical representation of the auxiliary ensemble for $n=4$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares three scenarios for classical information: pre-measurement, outcome-independent post-measurement, and adaptive post-measurement queries. It establishes a general method relating the optimal adaptive strategy to minimum-error discrimination on an auxiliary ensemble.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses fundamental limits in quantum communication protocols by showing that measurement back-action can be leveraged optimally through adaptivity, which is crucial for understanding resource limitations in quantum sensing and cryptography.

figures.caption: Figure 1. A scenario of query-assisted quantum state discrim- ination is illustrated. Bob sends a query to Alice, and Alice replies with a bit. The timing of the query and the classical information relative to the measurement significantly affects the optimal strategy and the achievable success probability. Both the query and the bit can be exchanged either before (red) or after (blue) the measurement. Interestingly, sending the query after the measurement can be more beneficial.
Figure 2. A graphical representation of the auxiliary ensemble for n = 4 is shown. The auxiliary ensemble consists of all pairwise mixtures of the original states.
